question: After a close play at 1st the batter-runner thinks they are out and walks across the dead ball line to the bench, but the umpire had actually called them safe. Can the batter-runner come back onto the field?
expected: No. Under 17.1 a runner who has left the diamond gives up the right to re-enter or take any further part in that at-bat innings; the Manual defines leaving the diamond as crossing the dead ball line. The only exception is a player sent off incorrectly by the umpire.

question: The base umpire wrongly calls a runner out at 2nd and the runner leaves the field. The umpires then realise the call was wrong. Can the runner return?
expected: Yes. 17.1 does not apply to players sent from the diamond incorrectly by the umpire; the Manual says that after an incorrect 'Out' call the player may be returned to the field.

question: A runner overruns 3rd base well into foul territory but stays inside the dead ball line, then comes back towards 3rd. Has the runner 'left the diamond' under 17.1?
expected: No. The Manual defines leaving the diamond as crossing the dead ball line, so 17.1 does not apply and the runner may continue. However, while off the base with the ball live, the runner can be put out by a tag (17.8).

question: The runner from 3rd steps over home plate without touching it and keeps running across the dead ball line to the bench. The plate umpire saw the miss. The catcher then holds the ball on home plate and appeals on that runner. What's the ruling?
expected: Runner out for missing the base and the run does not count (17.7), provided an umpire saw the miss and the fielder correctly identified the runner on the first appeal, before 'Play Ball' on the next batter. The runner cannot come back to touch home because they have left the diamond (17.1); the Manual says 17.1 exists to stop runners re-entering after missing home plate.

question: Between 1st and 2nd a runner deliberately pulls off their helmet, then keeps running and reaches 3rd safely. Nobody tags the runner before Time is called. Where does the runner end up?
expected: Back at 1st. Under 17.2 a runner who intentionally removes the helmet and is not put out before Time is returned to the last base they crossed before removing it. The Manual adds that the runner can only be sent back if the base(s) behind are unoccupied.

question: A runner rounding 2nd turns their head and the helmet falls off by itself. Is there any penalty?
expected: No. 17.2 only applies to intentional removal; the Manual says a helmet that falls off when a runner tilts their head while rounding a base has not been intentionally removed. Play continues normally.

question: A runner deliberately takes off their helmet while running and is then tagged out before Time is called. Does the out stand, or does the runner just go back a base?
expected: The out stands. 17.2 only returns the runner if they are not put out before Time, and the Manual confirms that if a runner is given out for any reason while not wearing a helmet, the out counts.

question: A runner intentionally removes their helmet on the way to 3rd, but by the time Time is called the base behind them (2nd) is occupied by another runner. What should the umpire do?
expected: Leave the runner where they are, since the Manual says offenders can only be sent back if the bases behind are unoccupied, but at least warn them not to remove the helmet again. If the runner does it again, the umpire can warn that they may be given out under rule 1.1(i) (safe playing environment). The Manual says rule 15(d) and (e) may also be considered.

question: A runner is standing on 1st (they have stopped running) when a throw goes over the dead ball line. What is the runner awarded?
expected: 2nd base. Under 17.3 runners get the next base from where they were when the thrown ball crossed the dead ball line; the Manual says a runner standing on 1st goes to 2nd even if they had stopped running.

question: The batter-runner is one step short of 1st when the throw to 1st sails over the dead ball line. Where does the batter-runner go?
expected: Only to 1st. The award is the next base from where the runner was when the ball crossed the line (17.3). The Manual says a runner one step short of 1st only gets 1st.

question: Runners on 2nd and 3rd. On the hit, the throw home goes over the dead ball line. At that moment the runner from 3rd is halfway home and the runner from 2nd is just short of 3rd. Where do the runners end up?
expected: The runner from 3rd scores and the runner from 2nd stops at 3rd (Manual 17.3 Scenario 2). Each runner gets the next base from where they were when the ball crossed the line (17.3), and for the runner from 2nd that next base is 3rd.

question: A runner misses 2nd base and is past it when an overthrow crosses the dead ball line. What is the runner awarded, and can the fielding side still do anything about the missed base?
expected: The runner still gets the next base from where they are, and the umpire gives no sign of the missed base. If the runner does not go back and touch the missed base, the fielding side can still appeal in the normal way (17.7) until 'Play Ball' is called on the next batter (Manual 17.3).

question: The runner from 1st and the batter-runner are both between 1st and 2nd when a thrown ball goes over the dead ball line. How are the runners placed?
expected: Under the Manual's 17.3 exception, when two runners are on the same base path only the front runner goes on to the base they were going to (2nd). The back runner (the batter-runner) must return to the last base they crossed (1st).

question: When is a base considered 'legally crossed' by a runner?
expected: When the runner has touched it, or when the umpire calls 'Play Ball' on the next batter without any appeal having been made (17.3(i)). Until then the fielding side can appeal a missed base (17.7). The Manual says umpires must not say or indicate anything if they see a runner miss a base.

question: The runner on 2nd leaves the base before the batter hits the ball, and the batter hits a ground ball into the outfield. What's the ruling?
expected: Under 17.4 the umpires call 'Time, Dead Ball', all runners go back to their bases and the play doesn't count. There is no count on the batter, who bats again. The umpire warns the runner that if they leave early again in the same innings they will be called out.

question: A runner leaves 1st before the ball is hit and the batter's fly ball is then caught. Is the batter out?
expected: No. The infringement happened before the hit, so the ball is dead: the catch does not count and there is no count on the batter (17.4 note). Call 'Time, Dead Ball', send all runners back to their bases and warn the runner who left early.

question: A runner already warned for leaving 1st early leaves early again later in the same innings. What happens?
expected: That runner is called out (17.4). Leaving early still makes it a dead ball, so 'Time, Dead Ball' is called, the other runners return to their bases, and nothing from the hit counts.

question: In the 3rd innings, runner A was warned for leaving base early. Later in the same innings, a different runner (B) leaves early for the first time. Is runner B out?
expected: No. The out under 17.4 only applies when the same runner offends again in the same innings. Runner B gets a dead ball, all runners return, and runner B is warned. A warning to one runner does not carry over to teammates.

question: A runner left base before the hit, but the umpires were slow to call it and the fielders completed a double play. Do the outs count?
expected: No. The infringement came before the hit, so the ball is dead from that point and no outs or plays count (17.4 note). All runners return and the offending runner is warned (or called out if it's their second offence that innings). The Manual says to call 'Time and Dead Ball' quickly, before an out can happen, to avoid this situation.

question: On the second half of the run to 1st, the batter-runner runs inside the diamond and the catcher's throw to 1st hits the runner. What's the call?
expected: Batter-runner out. Under 17.5 the batter must run the second half to 1st outside the diamond, and if they don't and a play is made between home and 1st, they are called out. The Manual says the purpose is to avoid interfering with a throw from the catcher or a fielder at home.

question: The batter hits to deep outfield and runs the whole way to 1st inside the diamond. No play is made at 1st. Is there a penalty?
expected: No. 17.5 only gives the out if the batter-runner fails to run the second half outside the diamond AND a play is made between home and 1st. With no play there is no penalty, although runners should still be coached to run outside.

question: The batter-runner is inside the diamond on the second half to 1st. The catcher picks up the ball but doesn't throw because the runner is in the line of the throw. Out?
expected: Possibly; it is the umpire's judgement. The Manual says the throw does not have to succeed or even happen: if the umpire thinks the attempt may have been obstructed by the runner being in the way after halfway, the runner is out. Rule Book 17.5 wording is stricter ('if a play is made between home and first base'), so the umpire must judge that a play was being made. The Manual says a field umpire who sees it should discuss it with the plate umpire.

question: The batter-runner runs through 1st base, turns right into foul territory and walks straight back, but is tagged before getting back to the base. Out?
expected: No. 17.6 lets batter-runners run or slide through 1st as long as they return immediately. They are only out if they show intent to move towards 2nd and are tagged while off the base. The Manual recommends turning right, away from 2nd, to avoid any doubt.

question: After running through 1st, the batter-runner takes a couple of steps towards 2nd, stops, then heads back and is tagged before reaching 1st. What's the call?
expected: Out. Under 17.6 a runner who shows intent to move towards 2nd and is tagged off the base is out, and the Manual counts one or two steps towards 2nd as showing intent. This is a judgement call, so coaches have no right of appeal.

question: A runner from 1st overruns 2nd base by a few steps and is tagged before getting back. The coach says 'you're allowed to overrun a base.' Is the runner safe?
expected: No, the runner is out. The overrun allowance in 17.6 only covers batter-runners running through 1st base. A runner who overruns 2nd (or 3rd) is off base while the ball is live and can be tagged out (17.8).

question: The runner from 1st misses 2nd base on the way to 3rd, and the base umpire sees it. After the play, the 2nd baseman holds the ball, stands on 2nd and appeals, naming the runner. What's the ruling?
expected: The runner is out for missing the base (17.7). The appeal is valid because the fielder held the ball while touching the missed base, an umpire saw the miss, and the right runner was named on the first appeal. The Manual's call is 'Runner out for missing the base.'

question: The fielding coach is sure a runner missed 3rd, and the fielder appeals correctly with the ball on 3rd. Neither umpire saw the miss. Out?
expected: No. Under 17.7 an appeal is only allowed if either umpire saw the runner miss the base, and the Manual says an umpire must see the infringement to call it. The runner is safe.

question: Two runners passed through 2nd on the same play and one of them missed it (the umpire saw which one). The fielder appeals naming the wrong runner, then tries again naming the other runner. Out?
expected: No. 17.7 requires the fielder to correctly identify the runner on the first appeal. The Manual says the fielding side gets one chance with no process of elimination, so after a wrong first nomination the game goes on.

question: After 'Play Ball' has been called for the next batter, the fielding team realises a runner missed 2nd on the previous play and wants to appeal. Allowed?
expected: No, it's too late. Once 'Play Ball' is called on the next batter with no appeal made, the base is considered legally crossed (17.3(i)). The Manual says appeals must be made before 'Play Ball' on the next batter.

question: A runner misses 2nd and reaches 3rd. By the time the runner realises, a following runner is standing on 2nd. Can the runner go back to touch 2nd?
expected: No. Under 17.7 runners are not entitled to return to an occupied base, and any retouching must be done in reverse order. The miss stands, so the fielding side can still appeal at 2nd before 'Play Ball' on the next batter; the runner is out if an umpire saw the miss and the runner is correctly identified on the first appeal.

question: A fielder obviously didn't see a runner miss 1st, but the coach shouts 'get the ball and stand on the base' and then tells the fielder which runner to name. Should the umpire accept the appeal?
expected: Yes, if an umpire saw the miss and the runner named on the first appeal is correct. The Manual's special note says the coach is the teacher and the players are learning, so the umpire accepts a coach-prompted appeal and calls the runner out.

question: A fielder has the ball in the bare throwing hand and tags the runner with the empty glove. Out?
expected: No. Under 17.8 note (i) a tag is touching the runner with the ball, or with the hand or glove holding the ball. An empty glove doesn't count, and the Manual specifically warns umpires about this situation.

question: A fielder tags a runner off base, but the ball pops out of the glove as the tag is made. Out or safe?
expected: Safe. Under 17.8 note (iii) the fielder must still have control of the ball after the tag. Whether the fielder had control is the umpire's judgement and can't be appealed (Manual).

question: On a force play at 2nd, the fielder has a foot on the base and the ball trapped on the ground under the glove before the runner arrives. Out?
expected: No. Tagging a base requires being in control of the ball (17.8 note ii), and the Manual says a ball on the ground with a glove or hand over it is not under control; the ball must be in the glove or hand. The ball must also beat the runner (1.2a).

question: Runner on 2nd only (1st empty). On a ground ball, the 3rd baseman catches the throw and steps on 3rd before the runner gets there, but never touches the runner. Out?
expected: No. With 1st empty the runner from 2nd isn't forced (17.9), so on a non-forced play the runner must be tagged before reaching the base (17.8b). Touching the base alone only works on a force.

question: A fielder touches 2nd base with the bare hand holding the ball (feet nowhere near the base) before the forced runner arrives. Is that a valid base tag?
expected: Yes. Under 17.8 note (ii) tagging a base means touching it with any part of the body while in control of the ball, so a hand holding the ball counts. On a force (17.8a) that puts the runner out if the ball beats the runner (1.2a).

question: A fielder with the ball waits on the baseline and the runner deliberately barges into the fielder, knocking the ball loose. What's the call?
expected: Runner out. The Manual (17.8) says a runner who deliberately barges a fielder to knock the ball out of their grasp has committed interference and must be called out. Runners must not charge fielders (Manual 17.14, 20), and 17.14 lets the umpire nullify any advantage and give the player out in severe cases.

question: Runner on 1st, batter hits a ground ball. Is the runner on 1st forced to run?
expected: Yes. Under 17.9 a forced play happens when the batter becomes a runner and there is no empty base behind the runner. The batter must run to 1st, so the runner on 1st must advance to 2nd. They can be put out by a tag of 2nd or of the runner before they arrive (17.8a).

question: Runners on 1st and 3rd (2nd empty), ground ball. Which runners are forced?
expected: Only the batter-runner and the runner from 1st. The runner on 3rd isn't forced because 2nd base behind them is empty (17.9), so that runner can only be put out by being tagged before reaching home (17.8b).

question: Bases loaded, ground ball to the pitcher, who throws to the catcher. The catcher, holding the ball with a foot on home plate, receives it just before the runner from 3rd arrives. Out?
expected: Yes, a force out. With the bases loaded every runner is forced (17.9), so tagging home before the runner arrives is enough (17.8a). The ball must beat the runner and the catcher must have control (1.2a).

question: Runner on 1st, ground ball to the 1st baseman, who steps on 1st to put the batter out and then throws to 2nd. The fielder at 2nd touches the base before the runner from 1st arrives. Is the runner out?
expected: No. The Manual (17.9) says the force is removed once the batter-runner is put out before 1st (tagged, or 1st base touched). The runner from 1st is no longer forced, so touching 2nd isn't enough and the runner must be tagged before reaching 2nd (17.8b).

question: Runner on 1st, ground ball. The batter-runner reaches 1st safely, then the fielder at 2nd touches 2nd with the ball before the runner from 1st gets there. Force out?
expected: Per the Rule Book: yes. 17.9 defines a force as no empty base behind the runner, and the batter-runner is now on 1st, so the base tag puts the runner out (17.8a). The Manual (17.9) conflicts, saying the force no longer stands once the batter reaches 1st, which would require a tag of the runner. The Rule Book (Ed 8) takes precedence, but this is unresolved; tagging the runner works under either reading.

question: Runner on 2nd runs on the hit, and the fly ball is caught by the centre fielder. The throw goes to the 2nd baseman, who steps on 2nd while the runner is still heading back. Does the fielder need to appeal?
expected: No verbal appeal is needed; the runner is out. Under 17.10 a runner who left before the catch is out if they fail to retouch before they or that base is tagged by a fielder with the ball. The Manual says the fielder just needs control of the caught ball and to touch or run across the base. If the ball beats the runner back, call 'Out' and let play continue.

question: With 1 out, the runner on 1st stays on the base until a deep fly ball is caught, then runs to 2nd. Is that allowed, and how can the fielding side get the runner out?
expected: Yes. After any catch the ball is live and runners may advance at their own risk (17.11). The batter is out, so the runner isn't forced, which means they must be tagged before reaching 2nd (17.8b); touching 2nd isn't enough. The Manual notes this is common on deep outfield catches.

question: Runner on 3rd. A foul fly ball is caught in foul territory. Is the ball dead, or can the runner try for home?
expected: The ball is live and the runner may try for home at their own risk (17.11): any catch, fair or foul, in fair or foul territory, leaves the ball live. If the runner left 3rd before the catch, they must retouch 3rd before they or the base is tagged (17.10).

question: Runner on 1st runs on the hit and has already rounded 2nd when the fly ball is caught. What must the runner do to be safe?
expected: Go back and retouch 1st, retouching 2nd on the way, because retouching must be in reverse order (17.7). The runner must get back before they or 1st base is tagged by a fielder with the ball (17.10). Once back on 1st they may advance again at their own risk (17.11).

question: Runner on 1st left on the hit and is standing on 3rd when the fly ball is caught. The fielder with the ball touches 2nd base. Is the runner out?
expected: No. Under 17.10 the runner is out only if they, or the base they left (1st), are tagged before they retouch. Touching 2nd (or 3rd or home) has no effect. The fielding side needs to tag 1st or tag the runner.

question: No outs, runner on 3rd. The runner runs on the hit and crosses home before a deep fly ball is caught by the left fielder, who throws to the 3rd baseman. The 3rd baseman steps on 3rd with the ball before the runner comes back to retouch it. Does the run count?
expected: No. The runner left 3rd before the catch and didn't retouch before the base was tagged by a fielder with the ball, so the runner is out (17.10) and their run is cancelled. That makes two outs: the batter (caught) and the runner.

question: Runner on 1st left on the hit, the fly ball was caught, and the runner stayed at 2nd without going back. The umpire called Time before anyone tagged 1st or the runner. Can the fielding side still touch 1st to get the out?
expected: Under the Rule Book, the runner is safe at 2nd: tags only count while the ball is live (17.8), and Time makes the ball dead (11). The documents leave a grey area, though. The Manual (17.11) describes this out as an 'appeal', and missed-base appeals can be made until 'Play Ball' on the next batter, so some umpires may allow it. The Manual also says not to call Time on a catch unless the ball is in an infield position and all runners are near their bases.

question: Runner on 1st runs on the hit, but the outfielder drops the fly ball. Does the runner need to go back and retouch 1st?
expected: No. 17.10 only applies when the batted ball is caught. With no catch, the batter becomes a runner, so the runner from 1st is still forced to 2nd (17.9) and play continues normally.

question: On a long hit, the runner from 1st runs past the runner from 2nd between 2nd and 3rd. What's the ruling?
expected: The runner from 1st (the one who passed) is out (17.12). The Manual says only the passing runner is out; the runner who was passed carries on. Runners must stay behind the runner in front until that runner is given out.

question: A runner falls over between 2nd and 3rd, and the runner behind stops and helps them up, staying behind them. Is that allowed?
expected: Yes. The Manual (17.12) says a runner directly behind may assist a fallen runner back to their feet, or help them along, as long as they do not overtake them.

question: The lead runner is tagged out between 2nd and 3rd and is walking off along the baseline. The following runner runs past them. Is the following runner out for passing?
expected: No. Under 17.12 a runner is only out for passing the runner in front before that runner has been given out. Once the front runner is out, passing them is not a violation.

question: Two outs, runners on 1st and 3rd. On a hit, the runner from 3rd crosses home. The batter-runner touches 1st, then passes the runner from 1st before 2nd for the third out. Does the run count?
expected: Yes. The batter-runner is out for passing the runner in front (17.12), but that third out was neither on the batter-runner before touching 1st nor a force play. Under 17.13, runs scored before the third out count, so the run counts.

question: Two outs, runner on 3rd. Ground ball to shortstop; the runner from 3rd crosses home before the throw beats the batter-runner to 1st for the third out. Does the run count?
expected: No. Under 17.13(a) no runs score when the third out is made on the batter-runner before they touch 1st, even if the runner crossed home first. The Manual gives this exact case.

question: Two outs, runners on 1st and 3rd. On a ground ball the runner from 3rd crosses home, then the runner from 1st is forced out at 2nd for the third out. Run?
expected: No run. The third out was a force play, and 17.13(b) says no runs score on a play where the third out is a force play. This is the Manual's Scenario 1 under 17.13.

question: Two outs, runners on 2nd and 3rd (1st empty). The batter reaches 1st safely, the runner from 3rd crosses home, then the runner from 2nd is tagged out between 3rd and home. Does the run count?
expected: Yes, as long as the run crossed home before the tag. The runner from 2nd wasn't forced to go past 3rd, so the third out was a tag on a non-forced runner, not a force or an out on the batter-runner before 1st. Under 17.13, runs scored before the third out count.

question: One out, runners on 2nd and 3rd. The 2nd baseman throws to 1st to put out the batter (second out). The runner from 3rd crosses home, then 1st throws to 3rd and the runner from 2nd is tagged for the third out. Run?
expected: The run counts (Manual 17.13 scenario). The second out was a force, but the third out was a tag on a runner who was no longer forced, because the batter was out. Under 17.13, runs scored before a third out that is not (a) or (b) count.

question: Same as the last case, but the runner from 3rd crosses home a moment AFTER the runner from 2nd is tagged at 3rd for the third out. Run?
expected: No run. 17.13 only counts runs scored before the third out is made. Umpires need to watch whether home was crossed before or after the tag.

question: One out, runners on 2nd and 3rd. The shortstop throws to 3rd and the runner from 2nd is tagged (second out). The runner from 3rd then crosses home before the throw to 1st beats the batter-runner for the third out. Run?
expected: No run. The third out was made on the batter-runner before touching 1st (17.13a), which the Manual treats as a force play (17.13b). Even though the run crossed between the second and third outs, it doesn't count (Manual Scenario 2).

question: Two outs, bases loaded. The batter reaches 1st safely and the runner from 3rd crosses home. Then the 3rd baseman, holding the ball, steps on 3rd before the runner from 2nd arrives. Is that the third out, and does the run count?
expected: Per the Rule Book: the runner from 2nd is still forced (17.9: no empty base behind), so the base tag is a force out and no run scores (17.13b). However, the Manual (17.9) says the force ends once the batter reaches 1st, which would make the base tag invalid (a tag of the runner would be needed, and runs before it would count). The Rule Book takes precedence, but this conflict is unresolved.

question: An unforced runner from 2nd reaches 3rd at about the same time as the throw, but keeps running towards home, trying to draw a bad throw. What should the umpire do?
expected: Treat it as incitement running (Manual 17.14 Scenario 1). Any advantage is nullified and the runner returned to the base they had before it happened; any outs made stand. The umpire should at least warn the runner. This is a judgement call with no right of appeal.

question: A forced runner from 2nd keeps running to 3rd even though the 3rd baseman is holding the ball on the baseline in front of the base. Incitement?
expected: No. The Manual cautions not to treat a forced runner as an incited runner, and in Scenario 3 says the runner is entitled to try to reach 3rd: it's the fielder's choice to challenge the runner, and the fielder could simply tag the base. The runner still must not charge the fielder to dislodge the ball.

question: A base coach keeps sending runners on when the ball is already ahead of them, to force throwing errors. One runner nearly collides with a fielder. What penalties are available?
expected: Under 17.14 the umpire nullifies any advantage (returns the runner to the earlier base, outs stand) and should at least warn. In severe cases where injury could have occurred, the umpire can give the player out, or eject the coach if the coach called it, but the coach or player must have had at least one warning before ejection.

question: An unforced runner from 2nd sees the ball arrive at 3rd first, then speeds up and drops a shoulder to run through the fielder and knock the ball loose. Call?
expected: The umpire calls Time the moment this is seen and gives the runner out (Manual 15(e) scenario, 17.14). The ball was already at 3rd, so the runner was about to cause danger. Runners must not charge fielders to dislodge the ball; this is a judgement call.

question: A runner slides safely into 2nd and the base is knocked a metre out of position. The runner is standing on the moved base when a fielder tags them. Out?
expected: No. Under 17.15(a), if the runner's impact dislodges a base and the runner reached it safely, no play can be made on that runner at that base. The Manual calls it a 'safe haven'. The umpires refit the base after Time.

question: On the same play a base was dislodged, a following runner arrives at that base and stands on the moved base rather than the spot where it belongs. Protected?
expected: No. Under 17.15(b) a following runner is treated as touching or occupying the base only if, in the umpire's judgement, they touch or occupy the point marked for the dislodged base. The Manual says following runners don't get the same luxury, as a base coach can guide them.

question: A runner dislodges 2nd on arrival and is safe, then sets off for 3rd, changes their mind and is tagged before getting back to the marked spot of 2nd. Out?
expected: Yes. The 17.15 note says any attempt to advance beyond the dislodged base removes the runner's exemption while they are off the point marked for that base, so a tag off that point counts (17.8).

question: Between 2nd and 3rd, a runner swerves well wide of the running line to get around a fielder who is holding the ball and about to tag. Call?
expected: Runner out for deviating from the running line to avoid a tag (17.16). The Manual says call the out as soon as the illegal deviation happens, so fielders know they can move on to the next play.

question: Close to 3rd base, a runner slides under the fielder's tag and reaches the base. Legal?
expected: Yes. 17.16 note: a runner close to a base may try to slide under a tag. If the slide gets the runner to the base before the tag, they are safe.

question: Runner on 2nd with 1st empty is caught off base and turns back towards 2nd along the shortest line to avoid a tag. Is that deviating from the running line?
expected: No, that's legal. The 17.16 note lets runners who are not in a force situation turn back on the shortest line. The Manual says runners may run forward or backwards (if not forced) to avoid a tag; they just may not deviate sideways off their line.

question: On a ground ball, the forced runner from 1st sees a fielder with the ball ahead and turns back to 1st to avoid the tag. What happens?
expected: Turning back doesn't help a forced runner: the 17.16 note only allows non-forced runners to turn back. The runner stays forced, and the Manual says the fielder simply tags the base the runner is going to (2nd) to make the out (17.8a), or tags the runner.

question: A runner moves off the running line to go around a fielder who is fielding a ground ball. Out for avoiding a tag?
expected: No. The Manual (17.16) says moving off the running line to avoid interfering with a fielder fielding the ball is not avoiding a tag. The fielder has right of way on a batted ball (18.1), so the runner must go around, but must not deviate to avoid a tag if the fielder is in a position to tag.

question: A runner steps off the line to go around a fielder who is standing in the base path without the ball. Avoiding a tag?
expected: No. The Manual says the umpire must decide whether the fielder has the ball and is in a position to make a tag. A fielder without the ball can't tag, so this is not a 17.16 deviation. A fielder without the ball who impedes the runner may be obstruction (rule 20).
